title: Clock Skew, NTP, and Why Wall Clocks Can't Order Events
lesson:
Every machine has its own quartz clock, and those clocks drift, typically by tens of parts per million, which is milliseconds per day or more. NTP periodically corrects a machine against a time server, but the correction is only as good as the network path: expect offsets from under a millisecond on a good LAN to tens of milliseconds across the internet, and larger during network trouble. Two servers can therefore disagree about what time it is, and that disagreement is called clock skew.

Skew breaks designs that treat timestamps as a truth about ordering. With last-write-wins conflict resolution, a node whose clock runs 200 ms fast can overwrite a genuinely newer write from a node with an accurate clock, silently losing data. Lock leases and token expiry have the same weakness: a client that thinks its lease is still valid, because of its own slow clock or a long pause, may act after the lock service has already granted it to someone else. Safe designs pair leases with fencing tokens, monotonically increasing numbers that the protected resource checks.

Clocks can also jump. NTP may step the clock backward, and leap seconds have caused it to repeat or smear. For measuring durations and timeouts, use a monotonic clock, which only moves forward and is unaffected by NTP adjustments, and reserve the wall clock for display and coarse logging. Using wall-clock subtraction for elapsed time can produce negative or wildly wrong durations.

When ordering matters, use mechanisms that do not rely on synchronized wall time: logical or vector clocks, a single sequencer, or consensus. Some systems go the other way and bound the uncertainty instead. Google's Spanner uses TrueTime, which exposes a time interval with explicit error bounds, and waits out that uncertainty before committing so timestamps respect real-time order.

questions.prompt: Which clock should you use to measure how long an operation took?
options: The wall clock, since it is the most accurate
A monotonic clock, since it never jumps backward
Any clock, as long as NTP is running
questions.explanation: A monotonic clock is unaffected by NTP steps, so elapsed-time calculations stay non-negative and meaningful.

questions.prompt: With last-write-wins using wall-clock timestamps, a node with a fast clock can overwrite a genuinely newer write from another node.
questions.explanation: The fast node's write gets a larger timestamp even though it happened earlier, so it wins and the newer data is lost.

questions.prompt: The disagreement between two machines' clocks is called clock ____.
questions.explanation: Skew is the offset between clocks, and it makes timestamps from different machines unreliable for ordering.

questions.prompt: What protects a resource when a client acts on an expired lease because its clock or process paused?
options: Fencing tokens checked by the resource
questions.explanation: The resource rejects requests carrying a token older than one it has already seen, regardless of what any clock says.

questions.prompt: Order a lease-protected write safely using fencing tokens, earliest first.
items: The storage resource rejects the write if a higher token was already seen
The lock service grants the lease with an increasing token
The client sends its write along with the token
questions.explanation: The token is issued at grant time and checked by the resource on each write, so a stale holder is rejected.
